questions.question: Under MCP 2026-07-28, what must be true of the information a server needs to answer one request?
options: It is retrieved from a session record tied to the connection
It builds up gradually across several requests on one connection
It is fully contained in that one single request, nothing inferred
It is cached from the connection's opening handshake exchange
questions.explanation: MCP 2026-07-28 is a stateless protocol: every request is self-describing, and a server must not infer context from requests that arrived earlier, even on the same connection.

questions.question: A server just finished handling a client's third request on a long-lived HTTP connection. What may it assume about the fourth request on that same connection?
options: The same client capabilities declared earlier still apply to the fourth request
The connection itself now counts as an authenticated session for later requests
The same protocol version negotiated for the third request still applies
Nothing: the fourth request must supply its own version and capabilities again
questions.explanation: Servers must not rely on prior requests over the same connection for capabilities, protocol version, or identity; every request supplies that metadata in its own _meta field.

questions.question: Why does MCP 2026-07-28 make every request self-describing instead of relying on a connection-scoped handshake?
options: So any replica can answer it, and a retry is safe to send anywhere
So a server can safely skip validating capabilities on most requests
So a single server process can hold more concurrent connections open
So a client only has to authenticate once per application launch
questions.explanation: Because no state is tied to a specific process, any replica can serve any request, a retry is safe to send to a different replica, and load balancers need no session stickiness.

questions.question: A client opens one stdio connection and, without closing it, sends a request for user A followed by an unrelated request for user B. What does MCP 2026-07-28 say about this?
options: It is fine only if both requests share one authorization token
It is fine; an open connection is never a session or a conversation
It is invalid unless the server issues a new session identifier first
It is invalid; a stdio process may carry only one conversation
questions.explanation: An open connection, such as a stdio process, is not a conversation or session: clients may interleave unrelated requests on the same transport, and a server must not treat connection identity as a proxy for continuity.

questions.question: A server needs a shopping cart to survive across several tool calls. Which design matches SEP-2567 guidance for MCP 2026-07-28?
options: Store the cart under the client's connection identifier on the server
Keep the cart in server memory and trust the order requests arrive in
Return an opaque handle from a create tool and reuse it later
Ask the client to resend a session identifier on every cart request
questions.explanation: State that spans multiple requests must be referenced by an explicit identifier the client passes on each request: a server-minted handle returned from a creation tool and threaded through later calls as an ordinary argument.

questions.question: Which of these did MCP 2026-07-28 remove in order to make statelessness the default?
options: The tools/call method and its CallToolResult content list
The per-request _meta field and its protocolVersion value
The server/discover method and its supportedVersions list
The initialize handshake and the Mcp-Session-Id header
questions.explanation: 2026-07-28 removes the initialize handshake, notifications/initialized, and the Mcp-Session-Id header; per-request _meta with protocolVersion, and server/discover, are exactly what replaced them and remain current.
